title: Brown v. Tellermate Holdings Ltd., No. 2:11-cv-1122, 2014 WL 2987051 (S.D. Ohio July 1, 2014), adopted as modified, 2015 WL 4742686 (S.D. Ohio Aug. 11, 2015)
pub: United States District Court, Southern District of Ohio
author: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio (Kemp, M.J.; Graham, J.)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The case does not address AI capabilities, selective deployment or work redesign directly. It offers relevant analogical support for continued lawyer oversight and verification when using unfamiliar technology, but does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal AI proposition.
qs: Once again, it is not sufficient to send the discovery request to a client and passively accept whatever documents and information that client chooses to produce in response.

mo.t: AI privilege: Legal subject matter is insufficient
Delegated error: Client relief need not excuse counsel
Digital ethics: Existing duties extend to new media
Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Legal malpractice: Error alone cannot establish liability
Predictive coding: Mature automation still needs transparency
TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment

kp.k: Electronic discovery retains established duties of reasonable investigation
kp.d: These opinions concern electronically stored information (ESI), not AI. The magistrate judge held that technological unfamiliarity did not displace counsel’s obligations of cooperation, transparency, truthful representations, and reasonable investigation. The district judge subsequently upheld the findings of discovery misconduct. The source therefore supplies findings about lawyers’ responsibilities when handling digital systems rather than predictions about AI’s effects.
qs: the underlying principles governing discovery do not change just because ESI is involved.
That holds true whether the bulk of the information relevant to discovery is ESI or resides in paper documents.

kp.k: Counsel cannot passively accept clients’ discovery representations
kp.d: The magistrate judge found that counsel repeatedly asserted that Tellermate could not access or produce Salesforce information without interviewing the relevant users and administrators or adequately investigating contrary evidence. Rule 26(g) required reasonable inquiry, not merely transmission of the client’s assertions. Similar failures concerning documents from Frank Mecka’s prior discrimination claim showed that the problem extended beyond unfamiliarity with ESI.
qs: counsel cannot simply take a client’s representations about such matters at face value.
Once again, it is not sufficient to send the discovery request to a client and passively accept whatever documents and information that client chooses to produce in response.
Here, counsel apparently never identified the persons having responsibility for salesforce.com information

kp.k: Third-party hosting did not remove control over discoverable data
kp.d: The courts rejected Tellermate’s claims that Salesforce owned the relevant information or that the licensing agreement prohibited its production. Tellermate employees could access their information, including historical entries, and administrators had extensive access. The magistrate judge treated the data as Tellermate’s ESI notwithstanding its storage on a provider’s servers; the district judge likewise found the asserted production barriers false or irrelevant.
qs: it was never true, at any time, that Tellermate was under a contractual obligation not to access or use its own information uploaded to salesforce.com by its own employees
no cogent argument could have been made, based on its language, that Tellermate was legally prohibited from accessing and producing its own information in discovery

kp.k: Preservation required action, not assumptions about provider backups
kp.d: Despite an October 4, 2011 preservation letter, counsel did not direct relevant users to preserve Salesforce information and assumed, without confirming, that the provider maintained historical backups. A January 2014 inquiry revealed retention of only three to six months. Tellermate could have exported data or requested preservation earlier; its late January 2014 export could not establish the historical integrity of information beyond that retention window. The finding concerned unverifiable integrity, not proof that particular substantive entries had been altered.
qs: The problem with that approach, at least in this case, is that Ms. O’Neil apparently assumed, without verifying, that salesforce.com actually kept backup data.
3 to 6 months from the current date.
Like any litigation counsel, Tellermate’s counsel had an obligation to do more than issue a general directive to their client to preserve documents which may be relevant to the case.

kp.k: Search transparency and precise confidentiality designations matter
kp.d: Tellermate produced more than 50,000 pages after searching employee names and nicknames, including common names that retrieved substantial irrelevant material. It designated almost all the production attorneys’ eyes only without demonstrating particularized harm or subsequently correcting the overdesignation. The courts criticized both the failure to cooperate over search methods and the attempt to justify restrictive designations by production volume and generalized competitive concerns.
qs: the production included a very large number of irrelevant and nonresponsive documents.
Consequently, the “Document Dump” is but another example of how Tellermate and its counsel eschewed transparency and cooperation in the discovery process.
the showing of harm must be particularized, and cannot simply rest on conclusory statements.

kp.k: Misconduct exposed both client and counsel to financial liability
kp.d: The district judge upheld joint liability for the specified reasonable attorneys’ fees and expenses against Tellermate and its former counsel, Calfee. The court relied on discovery certification duties, unjustified opposition to discovery, violations of discovery orders, and unreasonable litigation conduct under 28 U.S.C. § 1927. It rejected simple miscommunication as an adequate account of the record, finding gross negligence and bad faith. The supplied opinions establish liability for fees, not a quantified award.
qs: The record further supports the finding that Defendant Tellermate’s failures, and those of its former counsel, were part of an ongoing pattern of discovery misconduct and that their actions were in bad faith.
Defendant Tellermate and its former counsel are therefore jointly liable for the attorneys’ fees identified by the Magistrate Judge in his July 1, 2014 Opinion and Order.

kp.k: The district judge narrowed the original evidentiary sanction
kp.d: The July 2014 order barred reliance on any performance-related reason for termination. In August 2015, the district judge upheld sanctions but found that the record did not support the magistrate judge’s assessment of the severity of prejudice. The district judge emphasized other business records and the plaintiffs’ firsthand knowledge, questioned Salesforce data’s practical comparative value, and noted the absence of evidence of material alterations to the plaintiffs’ accounts. The modified sanction barred Tellermate from using Salesforce records or criticizing the plaintiffs’ use of the application, permitted plaintiffs’ testimony about what preserved records would have shown, and provided for a conditional adverse-inference instruction. Tellermate could still defend termination on sales-quota grounds using independent evidence.
qs: concludes that the evidentiary sanction is overbroad.
While Defendant Tellermate failed to take any steps to protect the integrity of the Plaintiffs’ accounts, there is no evidence that any material changes or deletions were made.
In light of the foregoing, the Court concludes that a somewhat narrower evidentiary sanction would be sufficient to mitigate the prejudice suffered by the Plaintiffs and serve the goal of deterrence.

kp.k: Sanctions required distinguishing responsibility among separately represented entities
kp.d: The original opinion grouped Insperity with Tellermate for convenience when they shared counsel. The district judge removed sanctions against Insperity because the record did not establish its responsibility for the misconduct. Insperity did not possess the Salesforce or document-dump materials, had no obligation to produce those materials, and was not shown to control Tellermate. Shared representation and a business relationship did not establish shared discovery responsibility.
qs: Those documents were not in the possession of Defendant Insperity, and Defendant Insperity had no obligation to produce them.

Although the record establishes a business relationship between Defendant Insperity and Defendant Tellermate, it does not support the conclusion that Defendant Insperity controlled the actions of Defendant Tellermate.

kp.k: Default judgment required more than further discovery shortcomings
kp.d: The district judge affirmed denial of the plaintiffs’ second default-judgment motion concerning additional Mecka documents and delayed disclosure of a second insurance policy. Although the insurance nondisclosure supported an inference of bad faith, the court found no actual prejudice from that nondisclosure because the settlement demand was within the first policy’s limits. Limited prejudice, the availability of lesser sanctions, and notice considerations weighed against default judgment. The opinion distinguished this later misconduct from the more pervasive misconduct underlying the first sanctions order.
qs: the limited prejudice suffered by the Plaintiffs weighs heavily against a finding that default judgment is appropriate here.
The narrow finding of bad faith is in contrast to the pervasive bad faith conduct at issue in the Plaintiffs’ First Motion for Default Judgment.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no concrete claims or predictions about AI.
pts.d: The opinions concern electronic discovery, cloud-hosted Salesforce records, preservation obligations, counsel’s reasonable-inquiry duties, and discovery sanctions. They do not discuss artificial intelligence or attribute changes in legal services to AI. Their findings about electronic information and document searches should not be recast as AI claims.
